Kalshi lists a Bitcoin contract that closes every fifteen minutes. It is a clean
forecasting problem with a public scoreboard: the market publishes a probability, the
world publishes an answer, and you can check yourself against both. I spent a while
trying to beat it.

I did not beat it. This post is the audit that convinced me, because the interesting part
turned out not to be the answer but how much work it took to trust it. Twice along the way
I had a result that looked like an edge, and both times the edge was a property of my own
measurement rather than of Bitcoin.

## What is actually being bet on

Start with the contract, because the phrasing hides something.

Settlement is **not** the last price. `settle_value` is the mean of the index over the 60
whole seconds before close. And the strike is not a round number someone chose — it is
*exactly the previous window's settle value*. So the question the market is really asking
is:

> Will the next 60-second mean land above the previous 60-second mean?

Both sides are 60-second averages of the same series. The strike is fixed and known the
instant the window opens, and the only random quantity is where the next average lands.
This is why every market opens near a coin flip: it is a random walk asked whether it will
end up above where it just was.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 150,
  fig.align = "center"
)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(arrow)
  library(slider)
  library(patchwork)
  library(tidyverse)
})
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35", size = 10),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)
pal <- c(
  idx = "grey45",
  settle = "#2C7FB8",
  market = "#E6812A",
  bad = "#B2182B"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: load
#| code-summary: "Show data loading"

# The tick data lives in a separate private repo and is far too large to duplicate,
# so the path is configurable. Quarto's freeze caches results, so the rendered post
# does not need the data present.
data_root <- Sys.getenv("KALSHI_TP_BOT_DATA", "~/Desktop/kalshi-tp-bot/data")
coin_dir <- path.expand(file.path(
  data_root,
  "raw_market_data",
  "crypto",
  "btc"
))
if (!dir.exists(coin_dir)) {
  stop("Set KALSHI_TP_BOT_DATA. Looked in: ", coin_dir)
}

N_DAYS <- 30

avail <- list.files(coin_dir, pattern = "_ticks_.*\\.parquet$")
end_day <- max(
  as.Date(str_extract(avail, "\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}")),
  na.rm = TRUE
)
all_days <- seq.Date(end_day - days(N_DAYS - 1), end_day, by = "day")

window_files <- function(pattern) {
  f <- list.files(coin_dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  d <- as.Date(str_extract(basename(f), "\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}"))
  f[!is.na(d) & d %in% all_days]
}

# The feed ticks ~5x/second; settlement is defined on whole-second prints, so keep
# the first tick of each second.
slice_to_seconds <- function(df) {
  df |>
    arrange(time) |>
    mutate(time = floor_date(time, "second")) |>
    distinct(time, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

brti_ms <- window_files("_ticks_.*\\.parquet$") |>
  map(\(f) slice_to_seconds(read_parquet(f))) |>
  list_rbind()

markets_15min <- window_files("^settled_.*_markets_.*\\.parquet$") |>
  map(read_parquet) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  arrange(close_time) |>
  filter(horizon == "15min") |>
  distinct(ticker, .keep_all = TRUE) |> # the feed carries a few dup tickers
  mutate(
    close_time = with_tz(close_time, "America/New_York"),
    start_time = close_time - minutes(15),
    weekday = wday(start_time, label = TRUE)
  )

book_15 <- window_files("^book_.*\\.parquet$") |>
  map(read_parquet) |>
  list_rbind()
```

## Getting the alignment right, and proving it

Three details in assembling this decide whether anything downstream means anything.

**Each second belongs to a market by time interval, not by row adjacency.** It is tempting
to label rows by "which market closes next" using `lead()` and fill. That silently glues
the weekly Wednesday 3–5am ET maintenance halt into single 9,000-second windows carrying a
real ticker and strike. An interval join on `[start_time, close_time - 1s]` refuses to
label those seconds at all, which is correct — and they get dropped.

**Timestamps are ET throughout**, matching the market's own `close_time`, so that hour and
weekday agree with each other.

**The book join looks backward.** `closest(time >= book_time)` takes the last quote at or
*before* each second. The direction matters enormously: reverse the inequality and every
second without a trade silently borrows its "market price" from a trade that has not
happened yet.

```{r}
#| label: assemble
#| code-summary: "Show assembly"

brti_15 <- brti_ms |>
  slice_to_seconds() |>
  mutate(
    index = row_number(),
    time = with_tz(time, "America/New_York"),
    .before = 1
  ) |>
  left_join(
    markets_15min |>
      select(
        ticker,
        weekday,
        start_time,
        close_time,
        floor_strike,
        settle_value,
        result
      ) |>
      mutate(lb = start_time, ub = close_time - seconds(1)),
    by = join_by(between(time, lb, ub))
  ) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(start = time == lb, end = time == ub) |>
  left_join(
    book_15 |> rename(mkt_ticker = ticker, book_time = time),
    by = join_by(ticker == mkt_ticker, closest(time >= book_time))
  ) |>
  distinct(index, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  rename(yes_last = last_yes) |>
  mutate(
    spread = ifelse(is.na(yes_mid), 0, abs(yes_ask - yes_bid)),
    yes_mid = coalesce(yes_mid, yes_last)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(ticker)) # drop the maintenance-halt orphans

brti_15 <- brti_15 |>
  mutate(
    kalshi_value = slide_index_dbl(
      value,
      time,
      mean,
      .before = seconds(59),
      .complete = FALSE
    ),
    time_left = as.numeric(difftime(close_time, time, units = "secs")) - 1,
    d_log_value = log(value) - log(lag(value)),
    d_log_value = if_else(start, NA_real_, d_log_value) # don't difference across a gap
  ) |>
  mutate(diff_floor_kalshi = kalshi_value - floor_strike)
```

Now the part that makes the rest trustworthy. At the final second of a window, my rolling
60-second mean *is*, by construction, the quantity Kalshi settles on. If the tick slicing,
the interval join, or the rolling window were misaligned even slightly, this is where it
shows — and nowhere else. So it is an assertion, not a printout:

```{r}
#| label: settle-check
#| code-fold: false
settle_check <- brti_15 |>
  filter(end) |>
  summarise(
    n_windows = n(),
    mean_diff = mean(kalshi_value - settle_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abs_diff = max(abs(kalshi_value - settle_value), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
settle_check
stopifnot(abs(settle_check$mean_diff) < 0.01)
```

```{r}
#| label: window-stats
#| include: false
n_sec <- nrow(brti_15)
n_mkt <- n_distinct(brti_15$ticker)
```

Reproducing an exchange's own settlement number to a mean error of
`r sprintf("%.4f", settle_check$mean_diff)` USD across `r format(settle_check$n_windows, big.mark = ",")`
windows is the licence to interpret everything below. The window is `r N_DAYS` days:
**`r format(n_sec, big.mark = ",")` index-seconds across `r format(n_mkt, big.mark = ",")` markets.**

## D1 · How the index moves

Two questions at once: are the one-second increments predictable, and is their *size*
predictable?

```{r}
#| label: d1
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| code-summary: "Show code"

dl <- brti_15$d_log_value[!is.na(brti_15$d_log_value)]
band <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(length(dl))
acf_signed <- acf(dl, lag.max = 300, plot = FALSE)$acf[, 1, 1]
acf_abs <- acf(abs(dl), lag.max = 300, plot = FALSE)$acf[, 1, 1]

bind_rows(
  tibble(lag = 1:300, acf = acf_signed[-1], series = "signed increment"),
  tibble(lag = 1:300, acf = acf_abs[-1], series = "absolute increment")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(-band, band),
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[["settle"]], width = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Autocorrelation of 1-second index increments",
    subtitle = "Dotted = white-noise band. Direction is unpredictable; magnitude is very predictable.",
    x = "lag (seconds)",
    y = "ACF"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: d1-table
#| code-fold: false
pacf_abs <- pacf(abs(dl), lag.max = 300, plot = FALSE)$acf[, 1, 1]
tibble(lag = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300)) |>
  mutate(
    acf_absolute = round(acf_abs[lag + 1], 3),
    pacf_absolute = round(pacf_abs[lag], 3)
  )
```

Signed increments are near-white — the lag-1 autocorrelation is
`r round(acf_signed[2], 4)`, which at n = `r format(length(dl), big.mark = ",")` is about
`r round(acf_signed[2]/band)`× the white-noise band and so is real, but it is tiny.
There is no direction to trade here.

Magnitude is a different animal. The ACF of `|increment|` starts at
`r round(acf_abs[2], 3)` and is still `r round(acf_abs[301], 3)` at lag 300 — **it never
halves inside five minutes.** That is long-memory decay, and the partial autocorrelation
confirms the shape: it collapses from `r round(pacf_abs[1], 3)` to
`r round(pacf_abs[5], 3)` by lag 5 and to `r round(pacf_abs[300], 3)` by lag 300, meaning
almost all of that persistence is one slow-moving level rather than a chain of short
dependencies.

The modelling consequence is the opposite of what "volatility clusters" usually implies.
Because the curve is nearly flat from 10s to 300s, a **slowly-varying volatility level
captures nearly all of it**. Updating a volatility state every second buys very little.

## D2 · When it moves

Volatility is not stationary across the day, and this is free conditioning information.

```{r}
#| label: d2
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-summary: "Show code"

# realised vol scaled to a 15-minute window, in basis points
by_hour <- brti_15 |>
  filter(!is.na(d_log_value)) |>
  mutate(et_hour = hour(time)) |>
  summarise(bps = 1e4 * sqrt(900 * mean(d_log_value^2)), .by = et_hour) |>
  arrange(et_hour)
by_wday <- brti_15 |>
  filter(!is.na(d_log_value)) |>
  summarise(bps = 1e4 * sqrt(900 * mean(d_log_value^2)), .by = weekday) |>
  arrange(weekday)

p1 <- ggplot(by_hour, aes(et_hour, bps)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[["settle"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +
  labs(
    title = "By hour (ET)",
    subtitle = "Peaks on the US cash open",
    x = "hour",
    y = "vol per 15-min window (bps)"
  )
p2 <- ggplot(by_wday, aes(weekday, bps)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[["settle"]]) +
  labs(
    title = "By weekday",
    subtitle = "Weekends are quiet",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  )
p1 + p2
```

```{r}
#| label: d2-range
#| code-fold: false
c(
  quietest_hour = by_hour$et_hour[which.min(by_hour$bps)],
  busiest_hour = by_hour$et_hour[which.max(by_hour$bps)],
  hour_ratio = round(max(by_hour$bps) / min(by_hour$bps), 2),
  weekday_ratio = round(max(by_wday$bps) / min(by_wday$bps), 2)
)
```

A `r round(max(by_hour$bps)/min(by_hour$bps), 1)`× swing between the quietest and busiest
hour, peaking on the US equity open, plus a clear weekend lull. Any volatility model that
ignores time of day is leaving a factor of ~3 on the table before it fits a single
parameter. Hold that thought — D8 comes back to it.

## D3 · The curve that looks like a finding

This is the central diagnostic: how much uncertainty is left about `settle_value` as the
clock runs down, measured against the two anchors a live model could use — the raw tick,
and the trailing 60-second mean.

```{r}
#| label: d3-curve
#| code-summary: "Show code"

settle_curve <- brti_15 |>
  filter(!is.na(settle_value), time_left >= 0, time_left <= 899) |>
  summarise(
    sd_kalshi = sd(settle_value - kalshi_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_raw = sd(settle_value - value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = time_left
  ) |>
  arrange(time_left)

crossover <- settle_curve |>
  filter(sd_kalshi < sd_raw) |>
  slice_max(time_left, n = 1)

settle_curve |>
  pivot_longer(-time_left, names_to = "anchor", values_to = "sd") |>
  mutate(
    anchor = recode(
      anchor,
      sd_raw = "raw tick",
      sd_kalshi = "trailing 60s mean"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time_left, sd, colour = anchor)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = crossover$time_left,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey45"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = crossover$time_left,
    y = max(settle_curve$sd_raw) * 0.75,
    label = paste0("anchors cross at ", crossover$time_left, "s   "),
    hjust = 1,
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("raw tick" = pal[["idx"]], "trailing 60s mean" = pal[["settle"]])
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Uncertainty remaining about the settlement value",
    subtitle = "Clock runs down left to right; log scale",
    x = "seconds to close",
    y = "sd of (settle − anchor), USD",
    colour = NULL
  )
```

The anchors cross at **`r crossover$time_left` seconds**. Before that the raw tick is the
better predictor; after it the trailing mean wins, and by the final second it wins
overwhelmingly. The reason is mechanical rather than statistical: the trailing mean is
centred about 30 seconds in the past, so it is a stale estimate of *now* — but once its
window starts overlapping the actual settlement window, it stops being an estimate at all
and starts being a partial observation of the answer.

Now the trap. Fit a power law to that curve and you get an exponent well above the 0.5 a
random walk implies:

```{r}
#| label: d3-slope
#| code-fold: false
slope_fit <- lm(
  log(sd_kalshi) ~ log(time_left),
  data = settle_curve |> filter(time_left >= 120, time_left <= 899)
)
round(coef(slope_fit)[["log(time_left)"]], 3)
```

An exponent of `r round(coef(slope_fit)[["log(time_left)"]], 3)` reads as *super-diffusion*
— variance growing faster than linearly in time, which would be a genuine exploitable
departure from a random walk and would justify a trend state in the model.

It is an artefact. The clean way to ask whether Bitcoin itself is super-diffusive is to
measure the index directly, with no anchor and no settlement value to confound it:

```{r}
#| label: d3-structure
#| code-summary: "Show code"

cont <- brti_15 |> arrange(time) |> distinct(time, .keep_all = TRUE)
lv <- log(cont$value)
tt <- as.numeric(cont$time)

structure_fn <- map_dfr(
  c(1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 480, 900),
  function(h) {
    i <- seq_len(length(lv) - h)
    ok <- (tt[i + h] - tt[i]) == h # only true h-second gaps
    tibble(h = h, n = sum(ok), sd = sd((lv[i + h] - lv[i])[ok], na.rm = TRUE))
  }
)
exp_all <- coef(lm(log(sd) ~ log(h), data = structure_fn))[[2]]
exp_60 <- coef(lm(log(sd) ~ log(h), data = structure_fn |> filter(h >= 60)))[[
  2
]]

ggplot(structure_fn, aes(h, sd)) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["settle"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["settle"]]) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sd[1] * sqrt(h)), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 300,
    y = structure_fn$sd[1] * sqrt(120),
    colour = "grey35",
    size = 3.4,
    label = "dashed = exact random walk (slope ½)"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Structure function of the index itself",
    subtitle = "sd of the h-second move vs h — no anchor, nothing to confound it",
    x = "h (seconds, log)",
    y = "sd of log move (log)"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: d3-exponents
#| code-fold: false
structure_fn |>
  mutate(local_exponent = c(NA, diff(log(sd)) / diff(log(h)))) |>
  select(h, n, local_exponent) |>
  mutate(local_exponent = round(local_exponent, 3))
```

Globally the exponent is **`r round(exp_all, 4)`** (`r round(exp_60, 4)` for h ≥ 60), and
the local exponent sits flat on ½ from about 8 seconds out to 900. Bitcoin here is a
textbook random walk. The one deviation is at h = 2 and it is D1's tiny lag-1 momentum,
dead within a few seconds.

So where did 0.6 come from? From what `settle_value` **is**. It is the mean of the last 60
seconds, not a point. At `time_left = t` those 60 seconds sit *h = t−59 … t* steps ahead,
so `settle − value_t` is the average of 60 *overlapping* random-walk displacements. The
variance of that average is not σ²t; it lags t by roughly the window half-width, which
makes the fitted log-log slope exceed ½ and *decline* toward ½ as t grows. The whole
shape, including the decline, is 60-second averaging applied to a random walk.

This is the first of the two false edges, and it points the modelling in a simpler
direction rather than a fancier one: **no trend state, no mean-reverting component.** A
plain random-walk level plus the correct settlement-window arithmetic reproduces this
curve. The effort belongs in the volatility level and in the density, not in extra state
dimensions.

## D4 · Is the market well calibrated?

Before asking whether I can beat the price, it is worth asking whether the price is any
good. Snapshots at fixed `time_left` so each market contributes one row per horizon.

```{r}
#| label: d4
#| code-summary: "Show code"

HORIZONS <- c(870, 720, 600, 480, 360, 240, 120, 90, 60, 30, 20, 10)

snapshots <- brti_15 |>
  filter(time_left %in% HORIZONS, !is.na(yes_mid), !is.na(result)) |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(result == "yes"), p_market = yes_mid / 100)

calib <- snapshots |>
  filter(time_left %in% c(600, 240, 120, 60)) |>
  mutate(
    bucket = cut(
      yes_mid,
      c(-1, 1, 10, 25, 45, 55, 75, 90, 99, 101),
      labels = c(
        "0-1c",
        "1-10c",
        "10-25c",
        "25-45c",
        "45-55c",
        "55-75c",
        "75-90c",
        "90-99c",
        "99c+"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_price = mean(yes_mid),
    realised = 100 * mean(y),
    .by = c(time_left, bucket)
  ) |>
  mutate(gap_pp = realised - mean_price)

ggplot(calib, aes(mean_price, realised)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey55"
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = pal[["market"]], alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste0(time_left, "s to close"), nrow = 1) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 5), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Market calibration at four horizons",
    subtitle = "Point size = number of markets; dashed = perfect calibration",
    x = "market price (¢)",
    y = "realised settle rate (%)"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: d4-summary
#| code-fold: false
calib |>
  summarise(
    cells = n(),
    median_abs_gap_pp = round(median(abs(gap_pp)), 2),
    n_weighted_abs_gap_pp = round(weighted.mean(abs(gap_pp), n), 2),
    pct_of_rows_within_3pp = round(100 * weighted.mean(abs(gap_pp) < 3, n), 1)
  )
```

The median cell misses by about a percentage point, and
`r round(100 * weighted.mean(abs(calib$gap_pp) < 3, calib$n), 0)`% of markets sit in cells
within 3pp of the diagonal. The few larger misses are all small-n cells at short horizons,
where almost everything has already resolved to the extremes. This price is honest across
the whole range, including the cheap tails that are easiest to fool yourself about.

## D6 · The headline test

Now the real question. Build the most defensible simple model this data supports — a
random walk, using D3's finding — and score it against the market at twelve horizons
spanning the entire 900-second window.

The model's state is one number: how many standard deviations of remaining move the index
currently sits above the strike.

```{r}
#| label: d6
#| code-summary: "Show the model and scoring"

scored <- snapshots |>
  mutate(
    sd_remaining = settle_curve$sd_kalshi[match(
      time_left,
      settle_curve$time_left
    )],
    z = diff_floor_kalshi / sd_remaining,
    p_model = pnorm(z)
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(z))

clamp <- function(p, eps = 1e-6) pmin(pmax(p, eps), 1 - eps)

scorecard <- scored |>
  mutate(
    brier_mod = (clamp(p_model) - y)^2,
    brier_mkt = (clamp(p_market) - y)^2,
    ll_mod = -(y * log(clamp(p_model)) + (1 - y) * log(1 - clamp(p_model))),
    ll_mkt = -(y * log(clamp(p_market)) + (1 - y) * log(1 - clamp(p_market)))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    brier_model = mean(brier_mod),
    brier_market = mean(brier_mkt),
    brier_delta = mean(brier_mkt) - mean(brier_mod),
    t_stat = t.test(ll_mkt - ll_mod)$statistic,
    .by = time_left
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(time_left)) |>
  mutate(market_better = brier_delta < 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: d6-table
#| code-fold: false
scorecard |>
  mutate(
    across(c(brier_model, brier_market), \(x) round(x, 4)),
    brier_delta = round(brier_delta, 4),
    t_stat = round(t_stat, 1)
  )
```

**The market wins at `r sum(scorecard$market_better)` of `r nrow(scorecard)` horizons.**
Every t-statistic on the paired per-market log-loss difference is negative and large; each
market contributes one row per horizon, so these are independent observations and the test
is valid. This is not twelve coin flips landing the same way.

```{r}
#| label: d6-plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-summary: "Show code"
ggplot(scorecard, aes(-log10(time_left), brier_delta)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["bad"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["bad"]], size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -log10(HORIZONS), labels = HORIZONS) +
  labs(
    title = "How badly the model loses, by horizon",
    subtitle = "Brier delta (market − model). Below zero = the market is better. Log-spaced horizons.",
    x = "seconds to close",
    y = "Brier delta"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))
```

The shape matters as much as the sign. The gap is **non-monotone**: it peaks around 90–240
seconds and shrinks at both ends. Both ends are degenerate, for opposite reasons. Early on,
the strike is the previous window's settle, so the market opens as a near coin flip and
there is almost nothing to know yet. Late, nearly everything has resolved below 10¢ or
above 90¢ and both sides agree.

So the market beats the model *hardest in exactly the band where real information is being
priced* — which is also the band a live strategy would want to trade. That makes the
negative result stronger, not weaker.

One more thing worth stating plainly, because it looks like a flaw and is actually the
opposite. `sd_remaining` is read off the settle curve, which was computed from the realised
outcomes of these same markets. A live model could not do that — it would have to estimate
that variance from past markets and carry the estimation error. **So this is a random walk
handed the empirically optimal per-horizon variance in hindsight, and it still loses at
every horizon.** Taking the advantage away can only make it worse.

## D7 · The market does lag — and it still does not pay

One mechanism could survive all of the above. The index updates about five times a second;
the contract price only moves when a human or a bot notices. That absorption delay is a
real thing, and it is invisible at any timescale you would look at on a chart.

Does the index move over `[t−k, t]` predict the mid move over `[t, t+k]`?

```{r}
#| label: d7
#| code-summary: "Show code"
lag_tbl <- map_dfr(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20), function(k) {
  g <- brti_15 |>
    arrange(ticker, time) |>
    group_by(ticker) |>
    mutate(
      idx_back = log(value) - log(lag(value, k)),
      mid_fwd = lead(yes_mid, k) - yes_mid,
      idx_fwd = log(lead(value, k)) - log(value)
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(is.finite(idx_back), is.finite(mid_fwd), is.finite(idx_fwd))
  tibble(
    k = k,
    index_to_mid = cor(g$idx_back, g$mid_fwd),
    index_to_index = cor(g$idx_back, g$idx_fwd)
  )
})
lag_tbl |> mutate(across(-k, \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

There is a real lag, it peaks at 2–3 seconds, and it is gone by 10. And the second column
is the control that makes it believable: if `yes_mid` simply tracked the index, the index's
*own* momentum would manufacture this entire table. It does not — index-to-index momentum
is a one-second effect, dead by k = 2, while index-to-mid is still at its peak there. Two
different phenomena that happen to be similar in size.

That is a genuine inefficiency. It is also worthless to a taker:

```{r}
#| label: d7-economics
#| code-summary: "Show code"
brti_15 |>
  arrange(ticker, time) |>
  group_by(ticker) |>
  mutate(
    idx_bp = 1e4 * (log(value) - log(lag(value, 3))),
    mid_fwd = lead(yes_mid, 3) - yes_mid
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(is.finite(idx_bp), is.finite(mid_fwd)) |>
  mutate(
    bin = cut(
      idx_bp,
      c(-Inf, -6, -3, -1, 1, 3, 6, Inf),
      labels = c("< -6bp", "-6..-3", "-3..-1", "-1..1", "1..3", "3..6", "> 6bp")
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_mid_move_c = round(mean(mid_fwd), 3),
    sd_c = round(sd(mid_fwd), 2),
    .by = bin
  ) |>
  arrange(bin)
```

Two problems. The expected move is about ±0.2¢ against a spread of roughly 1¢ and noise of
2.7–3.9¢ — you pay a cent to capture a fifth of one. And **the sign inverts in both tails**:
the largest index moves are followed by mid moves in the *opposite* direction. It is
momentum in the middle and reversal in the extremes, which is not a stable signal.

The one configuration where a 3-second lag pays is market making — posting limit orders to
earn the spread rather than pay it, and pulling quotes on the index tick to avoid adverse
selection. That needs a real order book, which this reconstruction is not.

## D8 · Letting a machine look for what I could not specify

Every diagnostic so far tests a hypothesis I was able to write down. Correlation is
structurally blind to shapes — a parabolic top rises and falls symmetrically, so its net
linear autocorrelation is near zero even if the shape is perfectly real.

So: hand a gradient-boosted tree a multi-scale encoding of the recent path, and start it
**at the market's own price** via `base_margin`. That offset is what makes the test fair.
The model begins where the market is and can only score by adding information the market
lacks. A model that finds nothing should score exactly zero.

```{r}
#| label: d8
#| code-summary: "Show the feature build and fit"
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(xgboost))

lags <- c(1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1200, 1800, 3600)
d8 <- brti_15 |> arrange(time)
for (L in lags) {
  d8[[paste0("r_", L)]] <- log(d8$value) - log(lag(d8$value, L))
}
rng <- map(seq(0, 300, by = 30), \(k) lag(d8$value, k))
d8$rng_hi <- do.call(pmax, c(rng, list(na.rm = TRUE)))
d8$rng_lo <- do.call(pmin, c(rng, list(na.rm = TRUE)))

d8 <- d8 |>
  mutate(
    chan_pos = (value - rng_lo) / pmax(rng_hi - rng_lo, 1e-9),
    curve_60 = r_30 - r_60 / 2, # <0 = decelerating: the -x² top
    rv_300 = 1e4 * abs(r_300),
    moh = minute(time),
    hod = hour(time),
    dow = as.integer(weekday)
  ) |>
  filter(time_left %in% HORIZONS, !is.na(yes_mid), !is.na(result))

feats <- c(
  paste0("r_", lags),
  "chan_pos",
  "curve_60",
  "rv_300",
  "moh",
  "hod",
  "dow",
  "diff_floor_kalshi",
  "time_left",
  "volume"
)
d8 <- d8 |>
  mutate(
    y = as.integer(result == "yes"),
    p_market = yes_mid / 100,
    day = as.Date(time)
  ) |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(feats), is.finite))

# THREE-way split by day. Early-stopping on the evaluation set manufactures edge.
days <- sort(unique(d8$day))
n1 <- floor(length(days) * .6)
n2 <- floor(length(days) * .8)
part <- \(d) as.matrix(d[feats])
margin <- \(d) qlogis(pmin(pmax(d$yes_mid / 100, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4))
tr <- d8 |> filter(day <= days[n1])
va <- d8 |> filter(day > days[n1], day <= days[n2])
te <- d8 |> filter(day > days[n2])

mk <- function(d) {
  m <- xgb.DMatrix(part(d), label = d$y)
  setinfo(m, "base_margin", margin(d))
  m
}
set.seed(1)
fit <- xgb.train(
  list(
    objective = "binary:logistic",
    eval_metric = "logloss",
    max_depth = 4,
    eta = 0.05,
    subsample = 0.8,
    colsample_bytree = 0.8
  ),
  mk(tr),
  nrounds = 400,
  watchlist = list(valid = mk(va)),
  early_stopping_rounds = 30,
  verbose = 0
)
te$p_model <- predict(fit, mk(te))
```

```{r}
#| label: d8-result
#| code-fold: false
ll <- function(p, y) -mean(y * log(clamp(p)) + (1 - y) * log(1 - clamp(p)))
tt_d8 <- t.test(
  -(te$y * log(clamp(te$p_market)) + (1 - te$y) * log(1 - clamp(te$p_market))) -
    -(te$y * log(clamp(te$p_model)) + (1 - te$y) * log(1 - clamp(te$p_model)))
)
tibble(
  test_rows = nrow(te),
  logloss_market = round(ll(te$p_market, te$y), 5),
  logloss_model = round(ll(te$p_model, te$y), 5),
  difference = round(ll(te$p_market, te$y) - ll(te$p_model, te$y), 5),
  t_stat = round(tt_d8$statistic, 2),
  p_value = round(tt_d8$p.value, 3)
)
```

The model does not beat the market. It comes out very slightly **worse**, and that sign is
the tell. Because it starts from `base_margin = logit(yes_mid)`, a model that found nothing
would score exactly zero — not slightly negative. Landing a hair below zero is the
signature of mild overfitting: it learned structure in the training weeks that did not
survive into the test week. Whichever way you read it, the thing it did not do is add
information the market lacked.

The most interesting part is what it reached for:

```{r}
#| label: d8-importance
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-summary: "Show code"
xgb.importance(model = fit) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(Feature = fct_reorder(Feature, Gain)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Gain, Feature)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[["settle"]]) +
  labs(
    title = "What the model leaned on",
    subtitle = "Ranked by gain",
    x = "gain",
    y = NULL
  )
```

The long-horizon trend features and the time-of-day/day-of-week terms rank at the top. The
learner went straight for the multi-hour trend and for D2's volatility seasonality — the
two things a human would reach for, and both genuinely real. **They are already in the
price.** D2 showed the seasonality is real; D8 shows knowing it adds nothing, because the
market knows it too.

## What I take away

The headline is that a prediction market with fifteen-minute contracts on Bitcoin is
efficient with respect to everything I could measure from the index alone. That is a
negative result, and negative results are worth publishing when the measurement is good
enough to distinguish "no edge" from "I did not look hard enough."

What makes me believe this one:

- The model was **handed a hindsight advantage** and still lost at 12 of 12 horizons.
- It lost **hardest in the band where information is actually being priced**, not averaged
  away across uninformative horizons.
- The one real inefficiency I found — a 3-second absorption lag — is genuine, cleanly
  separated from a confound, and **economically dead** at a fifth of a cent against a
  one-cent spread.
- A learner given free rein and the market's own price as a starting point found **no
  edge** — if anything a small negative — while ranking exactly the features the hypothesis
  predicted.

The methodological lesson is the one I will actually carry forward, and it happened twice.
The settlement curve's exponent of 0.6 was real, reproducible, robust to the fitting
window — and meant nothing about Bitcoin, because it was a property of averaging rather
than of the process. The instinct to fit a power law and read a story into the exponent is
exactly the instinct that needed checking against a measurement with nothing to confound
it.

The honest boundary on all of this: the benchmark is a book reconstructed from executed
trades, not a true order book, and the endgame is where that reconstruction is thinnest.
The result survives at the horizon where the book is *best* — 870 seconds, where only a
small minority of rows are degenerate — which is the check that matters most. But
execution-side questions, and market making in particular, need real order book data before
they can be asked at all. That is the next measurement, and it is a different one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproducing this

Index and market data come from a private research repo and are not redistributed here.
The analysis reads from `KALSHI_TP_BOT_DATA`:

```bash
# in ~/.Renviron
KALSHI_TP_BOT_DATA=~/Desktop/kalshi-tp-bot/data
```

Quarto's `freeze: auto` caches executed results, so the post rebuilds from cache without
the data present. Window: `r N_DAYS` days, `r format(n_sec, big.mark = ",")` index-seconds,
`r format(n_mkt, big.mark = ",")` markets.
:::

```{r}
#| label: cover
#| include: false
cover <- ggplot(scorecard, aes(-log10(time_left), brier_delta)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["bad"]], linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["bad"]], size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
ggsave("img/cover.png", cover, width = 6, height = 3.6, dpi = 150, bg = "white")
```
